checkpoints: gcloud output cho thấy `tags.items` (network tag thật) rỗng, trong khi `labels` chỉ có `tag=iap-ssh` — đây chính là bằng chứng và nguyên nhân gốc của lỗi.

Phân biệt đúng hai khái niệm dễ nhầm và áp đúng vào đoạn Terraform: network tag (target cho firewall rule/route, khai báo qua argument `tags` của `google_compute_instance`) khác với label (key-value tổ chức/billing, khai báo qua `labels`, không liên quan firewall); `labels = { tag = "iap-ssh" }` chỉ là MỘT LABEL có key tên "tag", hoàn toàn không phải network tag.
Hệ quả: `target_tags = ["iap-ssh"]` của firewall rule chỉ khớp network tag, nên rule ingress SSH-từ-IAP không bao giờ áp dụng cho `app-vm`.
Mọi VPC trên GCP đều có rule ngầm định `deny ingress all` ở priority thấp nhất (65535), áp dụng cho traffic không khớp bất kỳ rule tường minh nào khác.
Kết hợp hai điều trên, `app-vm` hiện tại không nhận được SSH từ bất kỳ nguồn nào, kể cả từ chính dải IP của IAP proxy.
Cách sửa: thêm đúng argument `tags = ["iap-ssh"]` vào `google_compute_instance.app_vm` (không sửa `labels`), rồi `terraform apply`.
Cách verify: `gcloud compute instances describe app-vm --format="value(tags.items)"` phải trả về `iap-ssh` (không còn rỗng), sau đó thử SSH qua IAP lại phải thành công.
`google_project_iam_binding` is authoritative for the role: applying it sets the entire member list of `roles/viewer` on the project to exactly what's in `members`.
This means it deletes every other current member holding `roles/viewer` that isn't listed — including members added by module B/module C from other teams, entirely outside this PR's scope.
Because multiple different Terraform modules grant `roles/viewer` to different members on this one shared project, using `_binding` here is a "ticking time bomb."

The PR looks like it just adds one new viewer, but it actually silently revokes everyone else's viewer access, causing a "permissions mysteriously vanished" incident that's hard to debug because the Terraform diff doesn't clearly show who will lose access.

Correct fix: switch to `google_project_iam_member`, a non-authoritative resource that only adds the one (role, member) pair without touching any other member holding the same role — safe when multiple teams/modules grant the same role on the same resource in parallel.
Before merging, verify by running `terraform plan` and carefully reading the proposed changes.
If the plan shows it would delete any member outside this PR's intended change, that's a clear sign of misusing an authoritative resource.
Identifies the bug precisely: the config has an `allow` rule for egress port 443 only, and there is no `deny` rule at all for other ports.
States that every GCP VPC network has an implicit default rule of "allow all egress" at priority 65535, which applies automatically and is independent of any custom rule the teammate wrote.

Names the teammate's mistaken assumption explicitly: they believed the single 443 `allow` rule would implicitly close/block every other port, when in fact an `allow` rule only opens exactly what it lists and never closes anything by itself.

Proposes the concrete fix: add a second `google_compute_firewall` resource with `deny { protocol = "all" }`, using the same `direction = "EGRESS"` and `target_tags = ["locked-egress"]` as the existing rule.

Gets the priority ordering right: the new deny rule must use a larger priority number than the existing 443-allow rule (e.g. 1000 vs 900), since a larger number means lower precedence, so 443 traffic still matches the allow rule first.

Explains the general evaluation mechanism: GCP firewall rules are evaluated in ascending priority-number order and the first matching rule wins, which is why unmatched (non-443) traffic falls through to the next rule instead of being blocked outright by the 443 rule.
Gives a concrete verification step from an instance tagged `locked-egress`: curling an HTTP endpoint (port 80) must time out/be blocked, while curling an HTTPS endpoint (port 443) must still succeed.
Reserve a static external IP using `google_compute_address` with `address_type = "EXTERNAL"` — this is the fixed IP the third-party partner will allow-list.
Cloud NAT cannot stand alone like an AWS NAT Gateway — it must be attached to a `google_compute_router` (Cloud Router).
The Cloud Router's `bgp` block isn't needed here since this is NAT-only, with no on-prem/hybrid connection.

Set `nat_ip_allocate_option = "MANUAL_ONLY"` and point `nat_ips` at the reserved static IP, instead of `AUTO_ONLY` which would assign an ephemeral IP that changes over time and couldn't be reliably allow-listed.
Raise `min_ports_per_vm` from the default 64 to 256 so each VM starts with more source ports available for concurrent connections.
Enable `enable_dynamic_port_allocation = true` with `max_ports_per_vm = 4096` so NAT can grant additional ports on demand when a VM needs to exceed the minimum, instead of a rigid fixed allocation.
Enable `log_config { enable = true, filter = "ERRORS_ONLY" }` to catch `OUT_OF_RESOURCES` errors (a sign of port exhaustion) early, before users report the issue.
Verify from the third-party partner's side that the observed source IP exactly matches the reserved static IP, not each VM's own IP, proving SNAT is working correctly.

Diagnoses the log line as Cloud NAT port exhaustion (allocation_status = "OUT_OF_RESOURCES" tied to crawler-worker-7), explicitly ruling out an application bug or a random network glitch as the cause.

Explains the mechanism: default min_ports_per_vm = 64 gives each VM only 64 source ports for concurrent outbound connections, so once crawler-worker-7's concurrent connections exceed that ceiling, NAT refuses to allocate ports for new connections.
States the resulting symptom follows directly from that refusal: connections that can't get a port fail, which is why the outage presents as intermittent (not total) outbound failure.
Attributes the 2pm timing to a heavier-than-usual crawl batch (more URLs/domains at once) pushing past the 64-port ceiling at that moment, rather than to a configuration change that just happened.
Remediation priority 1: raise min_ports_per_vm to a level that fits the real crawl load, measured from logs rather than guessed.

Remediation priority 2: enable dynamic port allocation (enable_dynamic_port_allocation = true) with max_ports_per_vm so ports scale elastically instead of relying on a rigid fixed number, given that crawl load fluctuates heavily over time.
Remediation priority 3: if the above still isn't enough under extremely heavy load, add more nat_ips, noting each static IP adds roughly 64k more available ports to the NAT gateway.

Remediation priority 4: reduce connection fan-out on the crawler side itself (connection pooling, capping concurrent connections per worker, enabling keep-alive to reuse connections) instead of continuously scaling NAT resources to compensate for an app design that opens too many connections.

Verification step: monitor the NAT log_config through the same high-load window (or actively replay the crawl load) to confirm no more OUT_OF_RESOURCES lines appear for crawler-worker-7 or any other worker in the same subnet.
